Let \(p,q\) denote densities with respect to Lebesgue measure, and assume the usual support condition

\[
q(x)>0 \quad \text{whenever } f(x)p(x)\neq 0,
\]

so that the importance weight \(p(x)/q(x)\) is well-defined on the relevant support.

---

## (1) Unbiasedness

The importance sampling estimator is

\[
\hat\mu_q=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{f(X_i)p(X_i)}{q(X_i)}, 
\qquad X_i\stackrel{iid}{\sim} q.
\]

Then

\[
\mathbb E_q(\hat\mu_q)
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 
\mathbb E_q\left[\frac{f(X_i)p(X_i)}{q(X_i)}\right].
\]

For each \(i\),

\[
\mathbb E_q\left[\frac{f(X_i)p(X_i)}{q(X_i)}\right]
=
\int \frac{f(x)p(x)}{q(x)} q(x)\,dx
=
\int f(x)p(x)\,dx
=
\mu.
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{\mathbb E_q(\hat\mu_q)=\mu.}
\]

So the IS estimator is unbiased.

---

## (2) Variance of \(\hat\mu_q\)

Let

\[
W(X)=\frac{f(X)p(X)}{q(X)}, \qquad X\sim q.
\]

Then \(\hat\mu_q=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n W(X_i)\), with iid summands. Hence

\[
\operatorname{Var}_q(\hat\mu_q)
=
\frac1n \operatorname{Var}_q(W(X)).
\]

Now

\[
\mathbb E_q[W(X)^2]
=
\int \left(\frac{f(x)p(x)}{q(x)}\right)^2 q(x)\,dx
=
\int \frac{f(x)^2p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,dx.
\]

Since \(\mathbb E_q[W(X)]=\mu\),

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}_q(\hat\mu_q)
=
\frac1n
\left[
\int \frac{f(x)^2p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,dx-\mu^2
\right].
}
\]

---

## (3) Optimal proposal \(q\)

We want to minimize

\[
\int \frac{f(x)^2p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,dx
\]

over all densities \(q\). By Cauchy–Schwarz,

\[
\left(\int |f(x)|p(x)\,dx\right)^2
=
\left(\int \frac{|f(x)|p(x)}{\sqrt{q(x)}}\sqrt{q(x)}\,dx\right)^2
\]

\[
\le
\left(\int \frac{f(x)^2p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,dx\right)
\left(\int q(x)\,dx\right).
\]

Since \(\int q(x)\,dx=1\),

\[
\int \frac{f(x)^2p(x)^2}{q(x)}\,dx
\ge
\left(\int |f(x)|p(x)\,dx\right)^2.
\]

Equality holds when

\[
q(x)\propto |f(x)|p(x).
\]

Therefore the optimal proposal is

\[
\boxed{
q^*(x)=\frac{|f(x)|p(x)}{\int |f(u)|p(u)\,du}.
}
\]

The corresponding minimum variance is

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}_{q^*}(\hat\mu_{q^*})
=
\frac1n
\left[
\left(\int |f(x)|p(x)\,dx\right)^2-\mu^2
\right].
}
\]

In the important special case \(f(x)\ge 0\),

\[
q^*(x)=\frac{f(x)p(x)}{\mu},
\]

and then

\[
\frac{f(x)p(x)}{q^*(x)}=\mu
\]

is constant. Thus the optimal proposal has zero variance when \(f\ge 0\).

---

## (4) Importance sampling for \(P(Y\ge 3)\), \(Y\sim N(0,1)\), using \(q=N(6,1)\)

Here

\[
\mu=P(Y\ge 3)=\int_3^\infty \phi(y)\,dy,
\]

where \(\phi\) is the standard normal density.

Use proposal

\[
q(y)=\phi(y-6),
\]

i.e. \(Y_i\sim N(6,1)\). The IS estimator is

\[
\hat\mu
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 
\mathbf 1\{Y_i\ge 3\}\frac{\phi(Y_i)}{\phi(Y_i-6)}.
\]

Now

\[
\frac{\phi(y)}{\phi(y-6)}
=
\exp\left\{-\frac{y^2}{2}+\frac{(y-6)^2}{2}\right\}
=
\exp(18-6y).
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{
\hat\mu
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n 
\mathbf 1\{Y_i\ge 3\}\exp(18-6Y_i),
\qquad Y_i\sim N(6,1).
}
\]

A simple algorithm is:

```r
B <- 1000
n <- 100
est <- numeric(B)

for (b in 1:B) {
  y <- rnorm(n, mean = 6, sd = 1)
  w <- exp(18 - 6*y)
  est[b] <- mean((y >= 3) * w)
}

mean_est <- mean(est)
var_est  <- var(est)
mean_est
var_est
```

The true value is

\[
\mu=1-\Phi(3)\approx 0.001349898.
\]

For this proposal, the second moment is

\[
\mathbb E_q\left[
\mathbf 1\{Y\ge 3\}\left(\frac{\phi(Y)}{\phi(Y-6)}\right)^2
\right]
=
\int_3^\infty \frac{\phi(y)^2}{\phi(y-6)}\,dy.
\]

Compute

\[
\frac{\phi(y)^2}{\phi(y-6)}
=
e^{36}\phi(y+6).
\]

Hence

\[
\int_3^\infty \frac{\phi(y)^2}{\phi(y-6)}\,dy
=
e^{36}\int_3^\infty \phi(y+6)\,dy
=
e^{36}\{1-\Phi(9)\}.
\]

Numerically,

\[
e^{36}\{1-\Phi(9)\}\approx 4.8656\times 10^{-4}.
\]

Therefore, for \(n=100\),

\[
\operatorname{Var}_q(\hat\mu)
=
\frac1{100}
\left[
e^{36}\{1-\Phi(9)\}-(1-\Phi(3))^2
\right].
\]

Numerically,

\[
\boxed{
\operatorname{Var}_q(\hat\mu)\approx 4.85\times 10^{-6}.
}
\]

Thus over 1000 independent replicates of size 100, the reported sample mean and sample variance should be close to

\[
\boxed{
\text{mean} \approx 1.35\times 10^{-3},
\qquad
\text{variance} \approx 4.85\times 10^{-6}.
}
\]

The exact simulation output will vary with the random seed.

---

## (5) Better proposal than \(N(6,1)\)

From part (3), because here

\[
f(y)=\mathbf 1\{y\ge 3\}\ge 0,
\]

the zero-variance optimal proposal is

\[
q^*(y)
=
\frac{\mathbf 1\{y\ge 3\}\phi(y)}{P(Y\ge 3)}
=
\frac{\mathbf 1\{y\ge 3\}\phi(y)}{1-\Phi(3)}.
\]

Thus \(q^*\) is the standard normal distribution truncated to \([3,\infty)\):

\[
\boxed{
q^*(y)=\mathcal L\left(Y\mid Y\ge 3\right), \qquad Y\sim N(0,1).
}
\]

Under this proposal,

\[
\mathbf 1\{Y\ge 3\}\frac{\phi(Y)}{q^*(Y)}
=
1-\Phi(3),
\]

which is constant, so the estimator has zero variance.

Therefore, yes, a much better proposal than \(N(6,1)\) is the truncated standard normal on \([3,\infty)\). In practice, if one insists on using a normal proposal \(N(\theta,1)\), a much better choice than \(N(6,1)\) is approximately \(N(3.15,1)\), or simply \(N(3,1)\), because it places mass near the important boundary \(y=3\) instead of far out at \(y=6\).

In practice, if one insists on using a normal proposal \(N(\theta,1)\), a much better choice than \(N(6,1)\) is approximately \(N(3.15,1)\), or simply \(N(3,1)\), because it places mass near the important boundary \(y=3\) instead of far out at \(y=6\).
